summary: Post-2000 wave 2. Four person entries built under the 1920–2000 frame gain their later careers and fuller cores, with read evidence. Joan Wallach Scott gains Davis's acknowledged influence, her use of psychoanalysis and fantasy, her French-feminism and parity books (through Landes and Dean), the veil and secularism books as a contribution to postcolonial critique (through Laborde and Whitney), Laura Lee Downs's 1993 critique, her 2000 reply on class, her 2012 critique of psychohistory and the 2018 Theses on Theory and History. Roger Chartier gains his 1993 questions to Hayden White and White's 1995 rejoinder, his 2003 reassessment of the new cultural history (against reducing practice to discourse; doubting Hunt's coherence), Bourdieu and Certeau as named resources, his Collège de France chair (2007–2016) and his later studies of the mobility of texts. Eric Hobsbawm gains his 1993 Budapest lecture against national myth-making, the Age of… synthesis and Tony Judt's critique of The Age of Extremes, his economic-history core, and dated later books and readings to Evans's 2019 biography. Hayden White gains Paul's 2019 assessment of his place in philosophy of history and the philosophers' criticisms Paul reports, his intellectual-history work, his Holocaust emplotment essay, Cronon's use and dispute, and the practical past. Each ends with at least 10 edges and at least 20 dated points; unread books are attributed to named readers.
authorization: User, 2026-10-17: “we need to go back to everyone who kept working after 2000”; “anyone important enough to be featured in the main timeline should have more than one edge and more than one or two points on the timeline”. rationale: The four entries stopped at 1986 (Scott), 1989 (Chartier), 1983 (Hobsbawm) and 1973 (White) on the timeline, with one to three chronology points and none after 2000. Every new edge rests on the person's own words or a named reader's explicit statement, read in full or in part with pages; abstract-only, WebFetch-extracted, translated and metadata-only readings are labelled in the evidence notes, and unread books are attributed locally to their reviewers. No new edge repeats an existing endpoint/type combination; later work that would have duplicated an existing arrow (Scott → gender, Chartier → culture, Hobsbawm → marx) goes into roster works or an edge revision instead. Named critics without nodes are drawn through a group entry with the critic named in the text (Downs via women; Judt via political; Ricoeur, David Carr, Lorenz, Ankersmit and Runia via philhistory, as Paul reports them). Four edge revisions are made without retargeting: edge_678 and edge_322 (Hobsbawm), edge_644 (Gramsci → Hobsbawm) and edge_257 (critics → White) gain later witnesses. Retargets of Scott's older group edges, a Chartier–Darnton edge, Ginzburg and Moses arrows to White, and anything touching the capitalism debate are left out (see release/README.md).

edge_678.relationship: Defends the difference between fact and fiction against “postmodernist” fashions (“We cannot invent our facts”, 1993) and reads the coauthors’ manuscript of Telling the Truth about History (1994)
edge_678.evidence_note: The 1994 acknowledgments name his detailed reading while absolving all readers of responsibility for the conclusions. This records assistance, not agreement. Revision 1.147 adds his own 1993 words, read in full ("The New Threat to History", NYRB, 16 December 1993): "postmodernist" fashions "imply that all “facts” claiming objective existence are simply intellectual constructions. In short, that there is no clear difference between fact and fiction. But there is, and for historians, even for the most militantly antipositivist ones among us, the ability to distinguish between the two is absolutely fundamental. We cannot invent our facts." The passage is brief ("I need say little about the first of these responsibilities"); the lecture's main subject is the nationalist abuse of history (see the nationaltradition critique). A contribution on the side of facts, not a critique of the 1994 coauthors.

edge_644.evidence_note: The1974 review connects Gramsci to rebellion and organization while questioning the continuing value of the organic/traditional distinction. This supports qualified reception, not an unverified provenance claim for every earlier Hobsbawm book. Revision 1.147: the reception continues in How to Change the World (2011), where, as Eagleton reports (LRB, 2011, read), Hobsbawm "thinks that Gramsci is the most original thinker produced by the West since 1917". Eagleton reports this judgment within a paragraph of criticisms (of the book's handling of Althusser, feminism and Trotskyism), not as his own view; the book is unread.

edge_322.evidence_note: A specific contribution within a heterogeneous field. The individual and group links describe related levels of the same history, not independent evidence of several transmissions. Revised Bandits specifies culture, political power and responses to criticism; the narrative reply distinguishes analysis from presentation. Revision 1.147: his later histories of Marxism, How to Change the World (2011), are known through Eagleton's review (read): Hobsbawm "remains broadly committed to the Marxist camp", insists on Marx's debt to the utopians and denies that the Manifesto is deterministic. Eagleton's praise is qualified: Hobsbawm is "not at his sharpest in the realm of ideas", misreads how Althusser's followers treated Capital, and slights feminism and Trotskyism. The book is unread; no separate arrow is drawn.

edge_257.evidence_note: Criticism is attributed to particular participants, not to every historian or contributor to Beyond the Cultural Turn. Evans’s introduction also explicitly accepts White’s defense of scrutiny from outside the discipline. Jenkins draws on White while distinguishing their uses of discourse; criticism is not this whole entry’s position. Ginzburg 1992 body remains unchecked. Revision 1.147 adds a later witness: Perry Anderson's review of Ginzburg's Threads and Traces (LRB, 26 April 2012; WebFetch extraction) reports that "Hayden White, already criticised by Momigliano, is the King Charles's Head" of Ginzburg's defence of history "as an inquiry capable of attaining truths". Ginzburg's texts remain unread.

text_revisions.old: Develops gender as a historical analysis of social relationships and power. Her 1986 formulation connects symbols, normative claims, institutions and subjectivity while insisting on historical variation.
text_revisions.new: A historian of modern France who, after studies of women’s work and the family with Louise Tilly (1975, 1978), proposed gender as a historical analysis of social relationships and power (1986), connecting symbols, normative claims, institutions and subjectivity while insisting on historical variation, and questioned experience as self-evident evidence (1991). Gender and the Politics of History (1988) made her, in Laura Lee Downs’s words, “the spokesperson for gender history”; Palmer, Valverde and Downs contested her poststructuralism. Later books, presented here through their reviewers, trace French feminists’ paradoxes between the abstract individual and sexual difference (Only Paradoxes to Offer, 1996, as Landes reads it), the parity movement (Parité!, 2005, as Dean reads it), the headscarf ban (The Politics of the Veil, 2007, as Laborde reads it) and gender in the discourse of secularism (Sex and Secularism, 2017, as Whitney and O’Grady read it); Laborde finds the veil book’s normative premises unclear, and O’Grady objects that the later book holds nineteenth-century Europeans to present moral standards. In a 2018 interview Scott asked how to write a critique of secularism without rejecting it. Answering an AHR forum on her 1986 essay (2008), she insisted that gender is useful only as a question and explained her use of psychoanalysis and fantasy to keep it critical; her reply presents the forum’s reception as geographically and politically situated, quoting Heidi Tinsman, and disputes Joanne Meyerowitz’s reading of a change of direction, asserting continuity in her concern with sexual difference. With Ethan Kleinberg and Gary Wilder she called for a theorized “critical history” (2018); Knowledge, Power, and Academic Freedom (2019), in Robin Whitaker’s account, treats academic freedom as an ethical practice and holds that disciplinary practice is no power-free zone; she has also written on the claim that history will judge (2020).

text_revisions.old: Explains how textual forms, reading practices and collective representations shape social differences. His programme joins material bibliography to differentiated appropriation, critically reworks Annales and uses conceptual resources without accepting every formulation.
text_revisions.new: A historian of reading, the book and written culture in early modern Europe who explains how textual forms, reading practices and collective representations shape social differences. His programme, set out in “Le monde comme représentation” (1989), joins material bibliography to differentiated appropriation, critically reworks Annales and uses conceptual resources without accepting every formulation. In 1993 he put four questions to Hayden White, on language, tropology, the procedures of research and relativism before the Shoah; they are known here through White’s 1995 rejoinder. In 2003 he argued that practices cannot be reduced to discourse, doubted that the new cultural history was as coherent as Lynn Hunt had claimed, and described it as a space of debate that had moved away from “the illusions of the linguistic turn”. He held the Collège de France chair “Écrit et cultures dans l’Europe moderne” from 2007 to 2016; his inaugural lecture called the tide of digital textuality a major rupture in the history of written culture, as his reviewer Christian Jouhaud quotes it. Later books, known here through their reviewers, follow the mobility of texts: the lost play Cardenio between Cervantes and Shakespeare (2011) and Éditer et traduire (2021).

Lectures et lecteurs dans la France d’Ancien Régime (1987); “Le monde comme représentation” (1989); Les origines culturelles de la Révolution française (1990; English 1991); L’ordre des livres (1992; English 1994); “Quatre questions à Hayden White” (1993); On the Edge of the Cliff (1996); « La nouvelle histoire culturelle existe-t-elle ? » (2003); Inscrire et effacer (2005); Écouter les morts avec les yeux (Collège de France inaugural lecture, 2007); Cardenio entre Cervantès et Shakespeare (2011); The Author’s Hand and the Printer’s Mind (2013); Éditer et traduire (2021). Readings: White (1995); Jouhaud (2008, 2022); Boucheron (2014).

text_revisions.new: Darnton connects thought with the material and commercial work of producing and distributing books. Chartier’s later studies follow texts’ mobility across attributions, printed versions, genres and translations, in his reviewers’ accounts.

text_revisions.old: Studies labour, popular protest, capitalist transformation and national identifications across different scales. Cultural evidence and explanatory synthesis coexist; his responses to criticism revise some claims while retaining others.
text_revisions.new: A historian of labour, popular protest, capitalist transformation and nations, who studies cultural evidence and explanatory synthesis across different scales; his responses to criticism revise some claims while retaining others. After Primitive Rebels (1959) and Labouring Men (1964), his four Age of… volumes (1962–1994) became, for reviewers, a synthesis of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991; Tony Judt called The Age of Capital his greatest work and criticised The Age of Extremes for keeping the political categories of the 1930s (1995). With Terence Ranger he edited The Invention of Tradition (1983); in a 1993 lecture in Budapest he told historians to resist national myths as they formed and to hold to the difference between fact and fiction. Later books include On History (1997); the memoir Interesting Times (2002), which Perry Anderson read as a fifth volume of the same project: he finds in its explanation of remaining Communist after 1956 what most readers would see as integrity, while faulting its limited engagement with the political history of European Communism and its treatment of other Marxists; How to Change the World (2011), a history of Marxism, which Terry Eagleton credits with judiciousness while criticising its handling of ideas, including Althusser, feminism and Trotskyism; and the posthumous Fractured Times (2013).

text_revisions.old: Examines how emplotment, argument, and tropes organize historical accounts. Narrative form helps constitute an interpretation rather than merely decorating established facts. His work raises disputes about historical explanation and representation; it should not be reduced to the claim that evidence is irrelevant.
text_revisions.new: Examines how emplotment, argument and tropes organize historical accounts: narrative form helps constitute an interpretation rather than merely decorating established facts. As Herman Paul reads Metahistory (1973), it treats emplotment as one of the ways historians explain, not as a replacement for explanation. His work raises disputes about historical explanation and representation; it should not be reduced to the claim that evidence is irrelevant. He asked what limits govern responsible narratives of the Holocaust (1992, known here through quoted passages), answered Roger Chartier’s four questions about language, tropes, research and relativism (1995), and from 2010 argued, after Michael Oakeshott, for a “practical past” of memories, attitudes and values that people summon “to justify, dignify, excuse, alibi or make a case for actions” (Historein, 2010). Philosophers of history built on and contested his work: Paul (2019) calls it the field’s shared reference point, while Timmins (2011) doubts its impact on historians’ practice, and Ginzburg kept him as a target, as Perry Anderson reads Threads and Traces (2012).

text_revisions.new: “The Burden of History” (1966); Metahistory: The Historical Imagination in Nineteenth-Century Europe (1973); Tropics of Discourse (1978); “The Value of Narrativity in the Representation of Reality” (1980); The Content of the Form (1987); “Historical Emplotment and the Problem of Truth” (1992); reply to Chartier (1995); Figural Realism (1999); afterword to Beyond the Cultural Turn (1999); “The Historical Event” (2008); “The Practical Past” (2010); The Fiction of Narrative, ed. Robert Doran (2010); The Practical Past (2014). White’s analysis of historical narrative is a distinct contribution within debates grouped here as the linguistic turn. Readings: Paul (2011, through Timmins; 2019); Anderson on Ginzburg (2012); Spiegel (2013, 2018).

text_revisions.new: Metahistory’s formalist reading of selected nineteenth-century European works is one project, read here only in its introduction (pp. 1–11); the 1999 afterword also affirms a Marxian commitment. Narrative construction does not erase the distinction between historical and invented events. The 1992 Holocaust essay is represented by passages quoted by Claus and Marriott, an excerpt witness, not by its full argument. “The Practical Past” (2010) and the 1995 rejoinder to Chartier (in authorised Portuguese translation) are read in full. The 2014 book, The Fiction of Narrative, Figural Realism and Paul’s 2011 study are known through contents pages and named readers (Spiegel, Neves, Sanz Loroño, Timmins); the 2005 exchange with Dirk Moses is dated from metadata, and Moses’s argument is unread. The criticisms by Ricoeur, David Carr, Lorenz, Ankersmit and Runia are reported by Paul (2019).
